resources.string: Manage this network\'s peers, setup keys and groups from the phone. Needs an access token.
Peers, setup keys and groups of this network, through the server\'s API.
The admin panel sends a token only over HTTPS. This account\'s server is %1$s.
A token can do what you can

An access token acts with its user\'s full role: an owner\'s or admin\'s token can delete every peer and key. Prefer a service user with the role you need — User only reads — and a short expiry. The token is stored encrypted on this phone and is sent only to this account\'s management server.
A token is stored for this account. A new one replaces it.
Test the token first; Save stores it once the server accepted it.
The token could not be stored.
The panel stops working for this account until a new token is set. The token itself stays valid on the server: revoke it there if it is no longer needed.
Only look: no rename, delete or new keys. Every change also asks for the screen lock.
This phone has no screen lock, so the panel only reads: nothing could prove who asks for a change. Set a PIN, pattern or password to make changes.

Instead of a token, sign in with the account this device uses, in the browser. The answer is kept in memory only and lapses within hours. Whether the server accepts it depends on its sign-in setup; if it does not, the stored token is used.
The server rejected the stored token: it expired, was revoked or belongs to another account.
The server did not accept this device\'s sign-in. Use an access token.
The stored token can no longer be opened (the phone\'s key store was reset). Set it again.
The server could not be asked.
Set a screen lock to make changes.
Too many attempts. Try again later.
The unlock was not confirmed; nothing changed.
The server did not accept the credential.
Your role does not allow this.
Not found: it is gone, or this server does not have it.
Something else is in the way of this change.
Too many requests. Wait a minute and try again.
The server\'s answer could not be read (%1$s).
The server connection goes through a SOCKS5 proxy with a password, which the admin panel cannot use yet. Use an HTTP proxy or a SOCKS5 proxy without a password.
The server connection\'s proxy address is not valid. Check Settings → Connection.
The server connection goes through ByeDPI, which is not running. Start BirdSocks first.
Your role can only read: the panel is read-only.
This phone has no screen lock: the panel is read-only.
Read-only is on for this account. Change it under Access to the server.
Your role sees only your own peers.
The peer has to sign in again when the account\'s login period runs out. Applies to peers added by a user\'s sign-in, not by a setup key.
Its login has expired: it stays offline until someone signs in on it again.
The peer leaves the network at once and has to be added again with a new sign-in or setup key.
This is this device. It cannot be deleted from here; sign out in Settings instead.
Changes are off: read-only, no screen lock or your role.
Adds one peer, then stops working.
Adds peers until it expires or reaches its usage limit.
Peers added with this key are removed after 10 minutes offline.
Shown only now: the server keeps no copy.
QR code of the invite link
Scan it on another phone with BirdSocks to add this account there. Other NetBird clients take the key itself.
No new peer can join with it. Peers it already added stay.

This server has no link invites: they need the built-in identity provider.

The old link stops working; a new one is shown once.
The link stops working; nobody can join with it.
This link is shown once and kept nowhere. Copy it now; whoever has it can join.
A service user has no sign-in of its own: scripts and integrations use its personal access tokens, with the rights of its role.
An identity for scripts with the role %1$s; it does nothing until it has a token.
The service user and all its tokens are removed: scripts using them stop working.
Tokens marked expiring soon stop working within %1$d days: make new ones before then.
Whoever holds the token acts as %1$s (%2$s) through the API for %3$d days.
Anything signing in with this token is refused from now on.
This may be the token this panel signs in with. Deleting it signs the panel out; you will need another token to come back.
The server keeps only a hash: this token is shown once and kept nowhere. Copy it now.
The token this panel signs in with (%1$s) — %2$s. Make a new one and sign in with it.
This server does not keep network traffic events (they need NetBird Cloud with traffic logging on).
No account could be read with this credential.
Peers added by users must sign in again after the set time. Peers added with setup keys are not affected.
Peers added by users must sign in again when their login expires.
Peers stay signed in for good, whatever happens to the people who added them.
How long a peer added by a user stays signed in.
Peers must sign in again after %1$s.

Peers that stay offline too long must sign in again.
Peers keep their login however long they stay offline.
How long a peer may stay offline before it must sign in again.
Peers offline for %1$s must sign in again.
New peers wait for an administrator before they join the network.
New peers wait for an administrator\'s approval before they join.
New peers join at once, with nobody reviewing them.
Peers waiting now are let in, and every new peer joins without review.
People who sign up wait for an administrator before they can use the account.
New users wait for an administrator\'s approval.
Anyone who signs up gets in at once.
A peer whose hostname another peer already has is refused instead of being renamed.
A peer with a hostname already taken is refused.
A peer with a hostname already taken gets a numbered name.
Peers connect to each other only when traffic needs it, and drop idle connections.
Peers open connections only when needed and close idle ones.
Peers keep a connection to every peer they may reach.
Peers in the chosen groups may put their ports on the internet through the reverse proxy.
Peers in the chosen groups may publish their ports on the internet.

Only peers in these groups may publish their ports.
Peers in %1$s may publish their ports.

Regular users see only their own peers.
Regular users can see every peer, group and route of the account.
Users can sign in only through an identity provider, not with a local password.
Local passwords stop working: everyone signs in through an identity provider.
Users may sign in with a local password again.
Anyone without a working identity provider, possibly you, can no longer sign in.
Local sign-in asks for a second factor.
Local sign-in asks for a second factor.
A local password alone is enough to sign in.

Changing a user\'s auto-groups moves their existing peers too.
Changing a user\'s auto-groups affects only peers added later.

Users\' groups follow the claim in their identity provider\'s token.
Groups come only from what is set here.
The token claim that lists the user\'s groups, e.g. groups.
Groups are read from the claim %1$s.
Only users in one of these groups (names, separated by commas) may use the account; empty lets everyone in.
Only members of %1$s may use the account.
The addresses peers get. Changing it gives every peer a new address.
Every peer gets a new address in %1$s.
Connections drop while peers move, and anything that relies on the old addresses breaks.
The IPv6 addresses peers get in IPv6-enabled groups.
Peers get new IPv6 addresses in %1$s.
Peers in these groups also get an IPv6 address.
The domain every peer\'s name ends with, e.g. laptop.netbird.cloud.
Every peer name changes: bookmarks, scripts and certificates using the old names stop matching.
Routing peers resolve domain routes for the peers behind them.
Routing peers resolve the names of domain routes.
Each peer resolves domain routes itself.
Peers report the connections they make; the Events area shows them.
Peers report their connections to the server.

Traffic logs count bytes and packets.
Traffic logs record connections without counting.

The version clients update themselves to: a number, latest, or empty for none.
